nodes.name: Split Cartan modular curve
nodes.statement:
For a prime integer $p$, let $X_{\operatorname{split}}(p)$ be the modular curve defined over $\mathbb{Q}$ attached to the congruence subgroup of level $p$
$$
\Gamma_{\operatorname{split}}(p)=\left\{ \left (\begin{array}{cc}a &b\\c& d\end{array}\right)\in\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})\colon b\equiv c\equiv 0 \text{ or }a\equiv d\equiv 0\right\}\,.
$$
differentia: attached to the congruence subgroup of level $p$
nodes.statement_short: $X_{split}(p)$ is the modular curve of the split Cartan congruence subgroup $\Gamma_{split}(p)\subset SL_2(\mathbb{Z})$.

nodes.name: X_split(p) is isomorphic to X_0^+(p^2)
nodes.statement: It is well-known that  $X_{\operatorname{split}}(p)$ is isomorphic over $\mathbb{Q}$ to the modular curve $X_0^+(p^2):=X_0(p^2)/w_{p^2}$, where $w_{p^2}$ stands for the Fricke involution.
conclusions: $X_{\operatorname{split}}(p)$ is isomorphic over $\mathbb{Q}$ to the modular curve $X_0^+(p^2):=X_0(p^2)/w_{p^2}$
nodes.statement_short: $X_{split}(p)\cong_{\mathbb{Q}} X_0^+(p^2)=X_0(p^2)/w_{p^2}$, the quotient by the Fricke involution.

nodes.name: Genus of X_split(p)
nodes.statement: The genus of this curve is positive  when $p\geq 11$ and, in this case, it is at least $2$.
conclusions: The genus of this curve is positive
it is at least $2$

nodes.name: Automorphism group of split Cartan modular curves
nodes.statement:
Assume that the genus of $X_{\operatorname{split}}(p)$ is positive. Then,
$$\operatorname{Aut}(X_{\operatorname{split}}(p))=\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathbb{Q}}(X_{\operatorname{split}}(p))\simeq\left\{\begin{array}{cc} \{1\} & \text{if $p>11$,}\\[5 pt]
(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^2 & \text{if $p=11$.}\end{array}\right.
$$
conclusions:
$$\operatorname{Aut}(X_{\operatorname{split}}(p))=\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathbb{Q}}(X_{\operatorname{split}}(p))\simeq\left\{\begin{array}{cc} \{1\} & \text{if $p>11$,}\\[5 pt]
(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^2 & \text{if $p=11$.}\end{array}\right.
$$
nodes.statement_short: For positive genus, all automorphisms of $X_{split}(p)$ are defined over $\mathbb{Q}$; the group is trivial for $p>11$ and $(\mathbb{Z}/2)^2$ for $p=11$.

nodes.name: Twisted cusp form f_chi has level lcm(N,N'^2)
nodes.statement:
We recall that, for a normalized  newform $f=\sum_{n\geq 1} a_n q^n\in S_2(\Gamma_1(N))^{\operatorname{new}}$ and  a Dirichlet character  $\chi$ of conductor  $N'$, the function $$f_\chi:=\sum_{n\geq 1} \chi(n)a_n q^n$$
   is a cusp form in $S_2(\Gamma_1(\operatorname{lcm} (N, {N'}^2))$  (cf. Proposition 3.1 de \cite{Atkin}).
conclusions: is a cusp form in $S_2(\Gamma_1(\operatorname{lcm} (N, {N'}^2))$
nodes.statement_short: The twist $f_\chi=\sum\chi(n)a_nq^n$ of a newform of level $N$ by a character of conductor $N'$ is a cusp form of level lcm$(N,N'^2)$.

nodes.name: q-parameter
nodes.statement: Here, as usual, $q=e^{2\pi \,i\,z}$.

nodes.name: Twist newform f tensor chi
nodes.statement:
Let  $f\otimes \chi$ denote the unique normalized newform with $q$-expansion
$\sum_{n\geq 1} b_n q^n$ that satisfies
 $b_{\ell}=\chi(\ell) a_{\ell}$ for all primes  $\ell\nmid N\cdot N'$.
differentia: $b_{\ell}=\chi(\ell) a_{\ell}$ for all primes  $\ell\nmid N\cdot N'$
nodes.statement_short: $f\otimes\chi$ is the unique newform whose Hecke eigenvalues at good primes are $\chi(\ell)a_\ell$.

nodes.name: Level of f_chi versus f tensor chi
nodes.statement: If $f\otimes \chi$ is a newform of level $M$  and $f_\chi$ has level $M'$, then   $M|M'$.  Moreover, if $M=M'$, then $f_\chi=f\otimes\chi$.
conclusions: $f_\chi=f\otimes\chi$
$f_\chi=f\otimes\chi$

nodes.name: Set of normalized newforms New_N
nodes.statement: Let   $\operatorname{New}_N$  denote the set of normalized newforms in   $S_2(\Gamma_0(N))^{\operatorname{new}}$.

nodes.name: Fricke eigenvalue and New_N^+
nodes.statement: For $f\in\operatorname{New}_N$,   $\varepsilon(f)$ denotes  the eigenvalue of  $f$ under the action of the Fricke  involution $w_N$ and set $\operatorname{New}_N^+=\{f\in \operatorname{New}_N\colon \varepsilon(f)=1\}$.
nodes.statement_short: $\varepsilon(f)$ is the Fricke eigenvalue of $f$, and $New_N^+$ the newforms with $\varepsilon(f)=1$.

nodes.name: Space S_2(f) spanned by Galois conjugates
nodes.statement: For a cusp form $f=\sum_n b_n q^n \in S_2(\Gamma_0(N))$ such that   $\mathbb{Q}(\{b_n\})$ is a number field,  $S_2(f)$ denotes the $\mathbb{C}$-vector space  of cusp forms spanned  by  $f$ and its  Galois conjugates.

nodes.name: Shimura abelian variety A_f
nodes.statement: In the particular case that  $f\in\operatorname{New}_N$,     $A_f$ stands for  the abelian variety attached to $f$ by Shimura.

nodes.name: A_f is a quotient of J_0(N) with differentials from S_2(f)
nodes.statement: It is well-known that $A_f$ is a quotient of $J_0(N):=\operatorname{Jac} (X_0(N))$  defined over  $\mathbb{Q}$ and the  pull-back of $\Omega^1_{A_f/\mathbb{Q}}$  is the $\mathbb{Q}$-vector subspace of elements in  $S_2(f) dq/q$ with rational $q$-expansion, i.e. $S_2(f) dq/q\cap\mathbb{Q}[[q]]$.
conclusions: $A_f$ is a quotient of $J_0(N):=\operatorname{Jac} (X_0(N))$  defined over  $\mathbb{Q}$
the  pull-back of $\Omega^1_{A_f/\mathbb{Q}}$  is the $\mathbb{Q}$-vector subspace of elements in  $S_2(f) dq/q$ with rational $q$-expansion
nodes.statement_short: $A_f$ is a $\mathbb{Q}$-quotient of $J_0(N)$ and its regular differentials are the rational elements of $S_2(f)dq/q$.

nodes.name: End_Q(A_f) is a totally real field
nodes.statement: Moreover, the endomorphism algebra $\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb{Q}}(A_f)\otimes \mathbb{Q}$ is a totally real number field.
conclusions: the endomorphism algebra $\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb{Q}}(A_f)\otimes \mathbb{Q}$ is a totally real number field

nodes.name: Quadratic character chi and field K
nodes.statement: From now on, we assume  $p\geq 11$ and   $\chi$  denotes the  quadratic Dirichlet character of conductor $p$, i.e. the Dirichlet character  attached to the quadratic number field  $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{p^*})$, where $p^*=(-1)^{(p-1)/2}$.
also_stated_at: We recall that $K$ is the quadratic field $\mathbb{Q}( \sqrt{p^*})$, where $p^*=(-1)^{(p-1)/2} p$, and $\chi$ is the quadratic Dirichlet character attached to $K$ .
nodes.statement_short: Fix $p\ge 11$; $\chi$ is the quadratic character of conductor $p$, attached to $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{p^*})$.

nodes.name: Twisting by chi permutes newforms
nodes.statement: The map $f\mapsto f\otimes \chi$ is a permutation of the set $\operatorname{New}_{p^2}\cup\operatorname{New}_p$. Under this bijection, there is a unique newform $f$, up to Galois conjugation, such that $f=f\otimes \chi$ when $p\equiv 3 \pmod 4$.
conclusions: The map $f\mapsto f\otimes \chi$ is a permutation of the set $\operatorname{New}_{p^2}\cup\operatorname{New}_p$
there is a unique newform $f$, up to Galois conjugation, such that $f=f\otimes \chi$
The map $f\mapsto f\otimes \chi$ is a permutation of the set $\operatorname{New}_{p^2}\cup\operatorname{New}_p$
there is a unique newform $f$, up to Galois conjugation, such that $f=f\otimes \chi$

nodes.statement_short: Twisting by $\chi$ permutes $New_{p^2}\cup New_p$; for $p\equiv3$ mod 4 exactly one Galois orbit is fixed (the CM form).

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement:
Since    $f_\chi\in S_2(\Gamma_0(p^2))$ for $f\in\operatorname{New}_{p^2}\cup\operatorname{New}_p$ (cf. Theorem 3.1 of \cite{Atkin}),   the level of $f\otimes\chi$ divides $p^2$ and, thus, the map  is well defined. The injectivity follows from the fact that $(f\otimes\chi)\otimes\chi=f$.
The condition $f=f\otimes\chi$  amounts to saying that $f$ has complex multiplication (CM)  by the imaginary quadratic field $K$ attached to $\chi$, i.e. $p\equiv 3 \pmod 4$,  and, moreover, $f$ is obtained from a Hecke character $\psi$ whose  conductor is the ideal of $K$ of norm $p$, which implies  $f\in\operatorname{New}_{p^2}$. Since $f$ has trivial Nebentypus, the Hecke character $\psi$ is unique up to Galois conjugation.
\hfill $\Box$
nodes.statement_short: Level bound from Atkin-Li gives well-definedness, involutivity gives injectivity; fixed points are CM forms from a unique Hecke character.

nodes.name: Map well defined
nodes.statement: Since    $f_\chi\in S_2(\Gamma_0(p^2))$ for $f\in\operatorname{New}_{p^2}\cup\operatorname{New}_p$ (cf. Theorem 3.1 of \cite{Atkin}),   the level of $f\otimes\chi$ divides $p^2$ and, thus, the map  is well defined.
nodes.statement_short: Atkin-Li level bound shows $f\otimes\chi$ has level dividing $p^2$.

nodes.name: Injectivity
nodes.statement: The injectivity follows from the fact that $(f\otimes\chi)\otimes\chi=f$.
nodes.statement_short: Twisting twice by $\chi$ is the identity.

nodes.name: Fixed points have CM
nodes.statement: The condition $f=f\otimes\chi$  amounts to saying that $f$ has complex multiplication (CM)  by the imaginary quadratic field $K$ attached to $\chi$, i.e. $p\equiv 3 \pmod 4$,  and, moreover, $f$ is obtained from a Hecke character $\psi$ whose  conductor is the ideal of $K$ of norm $p$, which implies  $f\in\operatorname{New}_{p^2}$.
nodes.statement_short: A fixed form has CM by $K$, needs $p\equiv3$ mod 4 and lies in $New_{p^2}$.

nodes.name: Uniqueness
nodes.statement:
Since $f$ has trivial Nebentypus, the Hecke character $\psi$ is unique up to Galois conjugation.
\hfill $\Box$
nodes.statement_short: Trivial Nebentypus makes the Hecke character unique up to conjugation.

nodes.name: Twisting does not preserve Fricke eigenvalue
nodes.statement: The above map does not preserve the eigenvalue of the corresponding Fricke involution, i.e.   it may be that  $\varepsilon(f)$ and $\varepsilon(f\otimes \chi)$ are different.

nodes.name: Inner twists and endomorphism algebras of A_f
nodes.statement:
Let $f \in \operatorname{New}_{p^2}\cup \operatorname{New}_p$ without CM. If $f$ has an inner twist $\chi'\neq 1$, i.e. $f\otimes \chi'={}^{\sigma} f$ for some $\sigma\in G_{\mathbb{Q}}:=\mathrm{Gal} (\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q})$, then $\chi'=\chi$ because $\chi'$ must be a quadratic character of conductor dividing $p^2$.
In such a  case,  $\operatorname{End} (A_f)\otimes\mathbb{Q}=\operatorname{End}_K(A_f)\otimes \mathbb{Q}$ is a non commutative algebra. Otherwise, $\operatorname{End} (A_f)\otimes\mathbb{Q}=\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb{Q}}(A_f)\otimes \mathbb{Q}$ is a totally real umber field.
nodes.statement_short: A non-CM newform can only have $\chi$ as inner twist; then End$(A_f)\otimes\mathbb{Q}$ is noncommutative, otherwise totally real.

nodes.name: Endomorphisms of A_f for CM newforms
nodes.statement: If $f\in\operatorname{New}_{p^2}$ has CM, then the dimension of $A_f$ is the class   number of $K$, $A_f$ has all its endomorphisms defined over the Hilbert class field of $K$ and $\operatorname{End}_K(A_f)\otimes\mathbb{Q}$ is the CM field $\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb{Q}}(A_f)\otimes K$ which only contains the roots of the unity $\pm 1$ (cf. Theorem 1.2 of  of  \cite{gola011} and part (3) in Proposition 3.2 of \cite{Yang2}). Moreover, $f\in\operatorname{New}_{p^2}^+$ if, and only if, $p\equiv 3\pmod 8$ (cf. Corollary 6.3 of \cite{Yang1}).
conclusions: the dimension of $A_f$ is the class   number of $K$
$A_f$ has all its endomorphisms defined over the Hilbert class field of $K$
$\operatorname{End}_K(A_f)\otimes\mathbb{Q}$ is the CM field $\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb{Q}}(A_f)\otimes K$ which only contains the roots of the unity $\pm 1$
$f\in\operatorname{New}_{p^2}^+$ if, and only if, $p\equiv 3\pmod 8$
nodes.statement_short: For the CM newform of level $p^2$: dim $A_f=h(K)$, endomorphisms over the Hilbert class field, only roots of unity $\pm1$, and $\varepsilon(f)=1$ iff $p\equiv3$ mod 8.

nodes.name: Isogenies between A_f for twisted newforms
nodes.statement: For two distinct $f_1, f_2\in(\operatorname{New}_{p^2}\cup\operatorname{New}_p)/G_{\mathbb{Q}}$, the abelian varieties $A_{f_1}$ and $A_{f_2}$ are nonisogenous over $\mathbb{Q}$ and are isogenous if, and only if, $f_1\otimes \chi={}^{\sigma} f_2$ for some $\sigma\in G_{\mathbb{Q}}$ (see Proposition 4.2 of \cite{goji}) and, in this particular case, there is an isogeny defined over $K$.
conclusions: the abelian varieties $A_{f_1}$ and $A_{f_2}$ are nonisogenous over $\mathbb{Q}$
are isogenous if, and only if, $f_1\otimes \chi={}^{\sigma} f_2$ for some $\sigma\in G_{\mathbb{Q}}$
there is an isogeny defined over $K$
nodes.statement_short: Distinct $A_{f_1},A_{f_2}$ are never $\mathbb{Q}$-isogenous, and are isogenous (over $K$) iff $f_2$ is a conjugate of $f_1\otimes\chi$.

nodes.name: Splitting of J_0^+(p^2)
conclusions:
$J_0^+(p^2):=\operatorname{Jac} (X_0^+(p^2))$ splits over $\mathbb{Q}$ as the product
$(J_0(p^2)^{\operatorname{new}})^{\langle w_{p^2}\rangle}\times J_0(p)$
nodes.statement_short: $J_0^+(p^2)$ is $\mathbb{Q}$-isogenous to the product of $A_f$ over $f\in New^+_{p^2}\cup New_p$ up to Galois conjugacy.

nodes.name: Decomposition of J_0^+(p^2) into A_f
nodes.statement: J_0^+(p^2)\stackrel{\mathbb{Q}}\sim \prod_{f\in(\operatorname{New}_{p^2}^+\cup\operatorname{New}_p)/G_{\mathbb{Q}}} A_f\,.
nodes.label: split

nodes.name: Fricke eigenforms from oldforms of level p
nodes.statement: Each $f\in \operatorname{New}_p$ provides a vector subspace of $S_2(\Gamma_0(p^2))^{\operatorname{old}}$ of dimension $2$ genera\-ted by  $f(q)$ and $f(q^p)$. The normalized cusp forms $f(q)+p\,\varepsilon(f) f(q^p)$ and $f(q)-p\,\varepsilon(f) f(q^p)$ are eigenforms  for all Hecke operators $T_m$ with $p\nmid m$ and the Fricke involution $w_{p^2}$ with eigenvalues $1$ and $-1$ respectively.
conclusions: provides a vector subspace of $S_2(\Gamma_0(p^2))^{\operatorname{old}}$ of dimension $2$

The normalized cusp forms $f(q)+p\,\varepsilon(f) f(q^p)$ and $f(q)-p\,\varepsilon(f) f(q^p)$ are eigenforms  for all Hecke operators $T_m$ with $p\nmid m$ and the Fricke involution $w_{p^2}$ with eigenvalues $1$ and $-1$ respectively
nodes.statement_short: Each level-$p$ newform gives oldforms $f(q)\pm p\varepsilon(f)f(q^p)$ that are Hecke and $w_{p^2}$ eigenforms with eigenvalues $\pm1$.

nodes.name: Decomposition of regular differentials of J_0^+(p^2)
conclusions: \Omega^1_{J_0^+(p^2)}=\left(\bigoplus_{f\in\operatorname{New}_{p^2}^+/G_{\mathbb{Q}}}S_2(f(q))\frac{dq}{q}\right)\bigoplus\left(\bigoplus_{f\in\operatorname{New}_{p}/G_{\mathbb{Q}}} S_2(f(q)+p\,\varepsilon(f)f(q^p))\frac{dq}{q}\right)\,.
nodes.statement_short: Differentials of $J_0^+(p^2)$ split as $S_2(f)dq/q$ over $f\in New^+_{p^2}$ plus $S_2(f(q)+p\varepsilon(f)f(q^p))dq/q$ over $f\in New_p$.

nodes.name: Decomposition of regular differentials
nodes.statement: \Omega^1_{J_0^+(p^2)}=\left(\bigoplus_{f\in\operatorname{New}_{p^2}^+/G_{\mathbb{Q}}}S_2(f(q))\frac{dq}{q}\right)\bigoplus\left(\bigoplus_{f\in\operatorname{New}_{p}/G_{\mathbb{Q}}} S_2(f(q)+p\,\varepsilon(f)f(q^p))\frac{dq}{q}\right)\,.

nodes.name: Genera g^+ and g_0
nodes.statement: Let $g^+$ and $g_0$ be  the genus of the curves  $ X_0^+(p^2)$ and  $X_0(p)$,  respectively.

nodes.statement:
From the genus formula for these curves, one obtains the following values
$$
\begin{array}{c|c|c|}
p  &   g^+ &g_0\\ \hline\hline
p\equiv 1 \pmod{12} &\displaystyle{\frac{(p-1)(p-7)}{24}}   & \displaystyle{\frac{p-13}{12}}\\[6 pt]

 p\equiv 7 \pmod{12}  & \displaystyle{ \frac{(p-1)(p-7)}{24}  }&\displaystyle{\frac{p-7}{12}} \\[6 pt]
 p\equiv 11 \pmod{12} &\displaystyle{ \frac{(p-3)(p-5)}{24} } & \displaystyle{\frac{p+1}{12}}\\\hline
\end{array}
$$
conclusions:
$$
\begin{array}{c|c|c|}
p  &   g^+ &g_0\\ \hline\hline
p\equiv 1 \pmod{12} &\displaystyle{\frac{(p-1)(p-7)}{24}}   & \displaystyle{\frac{p-13}{12}}\\[6 pt]

nodes.statement_short: Table of $g^+$ and $g_0$ according to $p$ mod 12, from the genus formula.

nodes.name: Hyperelliptic split Cartan curves
nodes.statement:
Assume $p\geq 11 $. Then,
$X_{\operatorname{split}}(p)$ is hyperelliptic if, and only if,  $p=11$. Moreover, one has $$\operatorname{Aut} (X_{\operatorname{split}}(11))=\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathbb{Q}}(X_{\operatorname{split}}(11))\simeq
(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^2\,.
$$
conclusions: $X_{\operatorname{split}}(p)$ is hyperelliptic if, and only if,  $p=11$

one has $$\operatorname{Aut} (X_{\operatorname{split}}(11))=\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathbb{Q}}(X_{\operatorname{split}}(11))\simeq
(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^2\,.
$$
nodes.statement_short: For $p\ge11$, $X_{split}(p)$ is hyperelliptic only for $p=11$, where its automorphism group is $(\mathbb{Z}/2)^2$, all defined over $\mathbb{Q}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 1
nodes.statement:
Assume  $X_0^+(p^2)$ is hyperelliptic. By  applying Lemma 3.25 of \cite{BGGP}, we obtain  $g^+\leq 10$, which implies  $p\leq 19$. We have $g^+=2$ if, and only if,   $p=11$ and, thus, the curve $X_0^+(11^2)$ is hyperelliptic. For $p>11$,  on has $g^+>2$   and, moreover, $p>13$ because  $X_0^+(13^2)$ is a plane quartic (cf. \cite{Baran}).  Lemma 2.5 of \cite{BGGP} states that there is a basis $f_1,\cdots, f_{g^+}$ of $S_2(\Gamma_0(p^2))^{\langle w_{p^2}\rangle}$ with rational $q$-expansions satisfying
\begin{equation}
f_i(q)=\left\{\begin{array}{cr} q^i+ O(q^i)&\text{ if the cusp $\infty$ is not a Weierstrass point of $X_0^+ (p^2)$,}\\q^{2 i-1}+ O(q^{2i-1})& \text{otherwise.}\end{array} \right.
\end{equation}
Moreover,  for any  such a basis,  the functions on $X_0 ^+(p^2)$ defined by
$$
x=\frac{f_{g^+}}{f_{g^+-1}}\,,\quad  y=\frac{ q dx/dq}{f_{g^+-1}}\,,
$$
satisfy $y^2=P(x)$ for  a unique squarefree polynomial $P(X)\in\mathbb{Q}[X]$ which has  degree $2g^++1$ or $2g^++2$ depending on whether $\infty$ is a Weierstrass point or not. The first part of the statement follows from the fact that,  for $p=17$ and $p=19$,  the vector space $S_2(\Gamma_0(p^2))^{\langle w_{p^2}\rangle}$ does not have any bases as in (\ref{congq}).

Now, we consider  $p=11$. In this case, $|\operatorname{New}_{11^2}|=|\operatorname{New}_{11}|=1$. Let $f_1\in\operatorname{New}_{11^2}^+$  and let $f_2\in\operatorname{New}_{11}$. The newform $f_1$ is the one attached to the elliptic curve $E_1/\mathbb{Q}$ of conductor $11^2$ with CM by  $\mathbb{Z}[(1+\sqrt{-11})/2]$, and $f_2$ is the newform attached to an elliptic curve $E_2/\mathbb{Q}$ of conductor $11$ without CM.  Since $\varepsilon(f_2)=-1$, the cusp forms  $f_1(q)$ and $h(q)=f_2(q)-11 f_2(q^{11})$  are a basis of $S_2(\Gamma_0(11^2))^{\langle w_{11^2}\rangle}$. Take the following functions on $X_0^+(11^2)$
$$
x=\frac{h}{f_1}=1 - 2 q + 2 q^3 - 2 q^5 + O(q^5)\,,\quad y=-2 \frac{q\,dx/q}{f_1}=4 - 8 q^2 + 8 q^3 + 24 q^4 - 32 q^5+ O(q^5)\,.
$$
Using $q$-expansions, we get the following equation for $X_0^+(11^2)$:
\begin{equation}y^2= x^6 -7 x^4+11 x^2+11\,.
\end{equation}The maps $(x,y)\mapsto (\pm x,\pm y) $ provide a subgroup of $\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathbb{Q}}(X_0^+(11^2))$ isomorphic to $(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^2$. Since $\operatorname{Aut}_{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}(X_0^+(11^2))$ is a finite subgroup of $\operatorname{End}(E_1)\times \operatorname{End}(E_2)\simeq \mathbb{Z}[(1+\sqrt{-11})/2]\times\mathbb{Z}$, we have that it must be  a subgroup of $(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^2$, which proves the second part of the statement.
\hfill $\Box$
nodes.statement_short: Bound $g^+\le10$ via Lemma 3.25 of BGGP, rule out $p=13,17,19$ by $q$-expansion bases; for $p=11$ compute the genus-2 model and bound automorphisms by endomorphisms of $E_1\times E_2$.

nodes.name: Genus bound
nodes.statement: Assume  $X_0^+(p^2)$ is hyperelliptic. By  applying Lemma 3.25 of \cite{BGGP}, we obtain  $g^+\leq 10$, which implies  $p\leq 19$.
nodes.statement_short: Hyperellipticity forces $g^+\le 10$, hence $p\le19$.

nodes.name: Case p=11 hyperelliptic
nodes.statement: We have $g^+=2$ if, and only if,   $p=11$ and, thus, the curve $X_0^+(11^2)$ is hyperelliptic.
nodes.statement_short: $g^+=2$ exactly for $p=11$.

nodes.name: Exclude p=13
nodes.statement: For $p>11$,  on has $g^+>2$   and, moreover, $p>13$ because  $X_0^+(13^2)$ is a plane quartic (cf. \cite{Baran}).
nodes.statement_short: For $p>11$ genus exceeds 2, and $p=13$ gives a plane quartic.

nodes.name: Recall hyperelliptic basis criterion
nodes.statement:
Lemma 2.5 of \cite{BGGP} states that there is a basis $f_1,\cdots, f_{g^+}$ of $S_2(\Gamma_0(p^2))^{\langle w_{p^2}\rangle}$ with rational $q$-expansions satisfying
\begin{equation}
f_i(q)=\left\{\begin{array}{cr} q^i+ O(q^i)&\text{ if the cusp $\infty$ is not a Weierstrass point of $X_0^+ (p^2)$,}\\q^{2 i-1}+ O(q^{2i-1})& \text{otherwise.}\end{array} \right.
\end{equation}
Moreover,  for any  such a basis,  the functions on $X_0 ^+(p^2)$ defined by
$$
x=\frac{f_{g^+}}{f_{g^+-1}}\,,\quad  y=\frac{ q dx/dq}{f_{g^+-1}}\,,
$$
satisfy $y^2=P(x)$ for  a unique squarefree polynomial $P(X)\in\mathbb{Q}[X]$ which has  degree $2g^++1$ or $2g^++2$ depending on whether $\infty$ is a Weierstrass point or not.
nodes.statement_short: Recall the $q$-expansion basis criterion for hyperelliptic $X_0^+(p^2)$ and its model.

nodes.name: Exclude p=17,19
nodes.statement: The first part of the statement follows from the fact that,  for $p=17$ and $p=19$,  the vector space $S_2(\Gamma_0(p^2))^{\langle w_{p^2}\rangle}$ does not have any bases as in (\ref{congq}).
nodes.statement_short: No such basis exists for $p=17,19$, proving the first part.

nodes.name: Newforms for p=11
nodes.statement: Now, we consider  $p=11$. In this case, $|\operatorname{New}_{11^2}|=|\operatorname{New}_{11}|=1$. Let $f_1\in\operatorname{New}_{11^2}^+$  and let $f_2\in\operatorname{New}_{11}$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix the unique newforms $f_1$ of level $121$ and $f_2$ of level $11$.

nodes.name: Attached elliptic curves
nodes.statement: The newform $f_1$ is the one attached to the elliptic curve $E_1/\mathbb{Q}$ of conductor $11^2$ with CM by  $\mathbb{Z}[(1+\sqrt{-11})/2]$, and $f_2$ is the newform attached to an elliptic curve $E_2/\mathbb{Q}$ of conductor $11$ without CM.
nodes.statement_short: $f_1,f_2$ correspond to elliptic curves $E_1$ (CM) and $E_2$ (non-CM).

nodes.name: Basis of invariant forms
nodes.statement: Since $\varepsilon(f_2)=-1$, the cusp forms  $f_1(q)$ and $h(q)=f_2(q)-11 f_2(q^{11})$  are a basis of $S_2(\Gamma_0(11^2))^{\langle w_{11^2}\rangle}$.
nodes.statement_short: $f_1$ and $h=f_2(q)-11f_2(q^{11})$ span the $w$-invariant forms.

nodes.name: Equation of X_0^+(121)
nodes.statement:
Take the following functions on $X_0^+(11^2)$
$$
x=\frac{h}{f_1}=1 - 2 q + 2 q^3 - 2 q^5 + O(q^5)\,,\quad y=-2 \frac{q\,dx/q}{f_1}=4 - 8 q^2 + 8 q^3 + 24 q^4 - 32 q^5+ O(q^5)\,.
$$
Using $q$-expansions, we get the following equation for $X_0^+(11^2)$:
\begin{equation}y^2= x^6 -7 x^4+11 x^2+11\,.
\end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Compute the genus-2 model $y^2=x^6-7x^4+11x^2+11$.

nodes.name: Visible automorphisms
nodes.statement: The maps $(x,y)\mapsto (\pm x,\pm y) $ provide a subgroup of $\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathbb{Q}}(X_0^+(11^2))$ isomorphic to $(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^2$.
nodes.statement_short: Sign changes give a $(\mathbb{Z}/2)^2$ subgroup over $\mathbb{Q}$.

nodes.name: Upper bound on automorphisms
nodes.statement:
Since $\operatorname{Aut}_{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}(X_0^+(11^2))$ is a finite subgroup of $\operatorname{End}(E_1)\times \operatorname{End}(E_2)\simeq \mathbb{Z}[(1+\sqrt{-11})/2]\times\mathbb{Z}$, we have that it must be  a subgroup of $(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^2$, which proves the second part of the statement.
\hfill $\Box$
nodes.statement_short: Automorphisms embed in units of End$(E_1)\times$End$(E_2)$, so at most $(\mathbb{Z}/2)^2$.

nodes.name: q-expansion shape of the basis f_i
nodes.statement: f_i(q)=\left\{\begin{array}{cr} q^i+ O(q^i)&\text{ if the cusp $\infty$ is not a Weierstrass point of $X_0^+ (p^2)$,}\\q^{2 i-1}+ O(q^{2i-1})& \text{otherwise.}\end{array} \right.
nodes.label: congq

nodes.name: Splitting field of an abelian variety
nodes.statement: For an abelian variety  $A$ defined over a number field, we say that a number field $L$ is the splitting field of $A$ if it is the smallest number field where $A$ has all its endomorphisms defined.
differentia: the smallest number field where $A$ has all its endomorphisms defined

nodes.name: Splitting field of J_0^+(p^2)
nodes.statement:
Let $L$ be the splitting field of $J_0^+(p^2)$. If $p\equiv 3\pmod 8$, then
$L$  is de Hilbert class field de $K$. For $p\not\equiv 3 \pmod 8$, $L=K$ if  there exists
 $f\in\operatorname{New}_{p^2}^+\cup \operatorname{New}_p$ such that $f\otimes\chi\in\operatorname{New}_{p^2}^+\cup \operatorname{New}_p$, otherwise $L=\mathbb{Q}$.
conclusions:
If $p\equiv 3\pmod 8$, then
$L$  is de Hilbert class field de $K$

For $p\not\equiv 3 \pmod 8$, $L=K$ if  there exists
 $f\in\operatorname{New}_{p^2}^+\cup \operatorname{New}_p$ such that $f\otimes\chi\in\operatorname{New}_{p^2}^+\cup \operatorname{New}_p$, otherwise $L=\mathbb{Q}$
nodes.statement_short: The endomorphism field of $J_0^+(p^2)$ is the Hilbert class field of $K$ if $p\equiv3$ mod 8, else $K$ or $\mathbb{Q}$ depending on twists.
nodes.label: split

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2
nodes.statement:
On the one hand, for two distinct $f_1,f_2\in(\operatorname{New}_{p^2}^+\cup \operatorname{New}_p)/G_{\mathbb{Q}}$  without CM, $A_{f_1}$ and $A_{f_2}$ are isogenous if, and only if, $f_2$ is the Galois conjugate of $f_1\otimes \chi$  and, in this case, the isogeny is defined over $K$.

On the other hand, if  $f\in\operatorname{New}_{p^2}^+\cup\operatorname{New}_p$ does not have CM, then $f$ has at most $\chi$ as an inner twist. In this case, the splitting field of $A_f$ is $K$ or $\mathbb{Q}$ depending on whether $\chi$ is an inner twist of $f$ or not. If $f$ has CM, then the splitting field of $A_f$ is the Hilbert class field of $K$  and $A_f$ is unique.
  \hfill $\Box$
nodes.statement_short: Analyse isogenies between factors $A_f$ (twists by $\chi$) and the splitting field of each factor, separating CM and non-CM newforms.

nodes.name: Isogenies between factors
nodes.statement: On the one hand, for two distinct $f_1,f_2\in(\operatorname{New}_{p^2}^+\cup \operatorname{New}_p)/G_{\mathbb{Q}}$  without CM, $A_{f_1}$ and $A_{f_2}$ are isogenous if, and only if, $f_2$ is the Galois conjugate of $f_1\otimes \chi$  and, in this case, the isogeny is defined over $K$.
nodes.statement_short: Factors are isogenous iff related by twisting by $\chi$, over $K$.

nodes.name: Non-CM factors
nodes.statement: On the other hand, if  $f\in\operatorname{New}_{p^2}^+\cup\operatorname{New}_p$ does not have CM, then $f$ has at most $\chi$ as an inner twist. In this case, the splitting field of $A_f$ is $K$ or $\mathbb{Q}$ depending on whether $\chi$ is an inner twist of $f$ or not.
nodes.statement_short: A non-CM factor splits over $K$ or $\mathbb{Q}$ according to inner twist by $\chi$.

nodes.name: CM factor
nodes.statement:
If $f$ has CM, then the splitting field of $A_f$ is the Hilbert class field of $K$  and $A_f$ is unique.
  \hfill $\Box$
nodes.statement_short: The CM factor splits over the Hilbert class field of $K$ and is unique.

nodes.name: Automorphisms of X_0^+(p^2) are defined over K
nodes.statement: All automorphisms  of $ X_0^+(p^2)$ are defined over $K$.
conclusions: All automorphisms  of $ X_0^+(p^2)$ are defined over $K$
nodes.label: defi

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3
nodes.statement:
By Lemma \ref{split}, we only have to consider the case $p\equiv 3 \pmod 8$ and, by Proposition \ref{11}, we can assume $p>11$. Let $g_c$ be the dimension of the  abelian variety $A_f$ with $f\in\operatorname{New}_{p^2}$ having complex multiplication. We know that $g_c$ is the class number of $K$. Due to the fact that $g_c=(2V-(p-1)/2)/3$, where $V$ is the number of quadratic residues modulo $p$ in the interval $[1,(p-1)/2]$, we have $g_c\leq (p-1)/6$.  Since $g^+> 1+(p-1)/3$ for $p>11$ and $p\equiv 3 \pmod 8$, $g^+>  1+2 g_c$. Now, the statement is obtained  by applying  the same argument   used in the proof of Lemma 1.4 of \cite{KM}.
\hfill $\Box$
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $p\equiv3$ mod 8, $p>11$; bound the CM factor dimension $g_c\le(p-1)/6$ so $g^+>1+2g_c$, then apply the argument of Kenku-Momose Lemma 1.4.

nodes.name: Reduce to p = 3 mod 8, p>11
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{split}, we only have to consider the case $p\equiv 3 \pmod 8$ and, by Proposition \ref{11}, we can assume $p>11$.
nodes.statement_short: By Lemma 2 and Proposition 1 only $p\equiv3$ mod 8, $p>11$ remains.

nodes.name: Dimension of CM factor
nodes.statement: Let $g_c$ be the dimension of the  abelian variety $A_f$ with $f\in\operatorname{New}_{p^2}$ having complex multiplication. We know that $g_c$ is the class number of $K$.
nodes.statement_short: $g_c$ is the dimension of the CM factor, equal to the class number of $K$.

nodes.name: Bound g_c
nodes.statement: Due to the fact that $g_c=(2V-(p-1)/2)/3$, where $V$ is the number of quadratic residues modulo $p$ in the interval $[1,(p-1)/2]$, we have $g_c\leq (p-1)/6$.
nodes.statement_short: Class number formula gives $g_c\le(p-1)/6$.

nodes.name: Compare with g^+
nodes.statement: Since $g^+> 1+(p-1)/3$ for $p>11$ and $p\equiv 3 \pmod 8$, $g^+>  1+2 g_c$.
nodes.statement_short: Genus formula yields $g^+>1+2g_c$.

nodes.name: Apply Kenku-Momose argument
nodes.statement:
Now, the statement is obtained  by applying  the same argument   used in the proof of Lemma 1.4 of \cite{KM}.
\hfill $\Box$
nodes.statement_short: Conclude with the argument of Lemma 1.4 of Kenku-Momose.

nodes.name: Rational automorphism group is elementary abelian 2-group
nodes.statement: The group $ \operatorname{Aut}_{\mathbb{Q}} (X_0^+(p^2))$ is isomorphic to $(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^s$ for some integer $s\geq 0$.
conclusions: The group $ \operatorname{Aut}_{\mathbb{Q}} (X_0^+(p^2))$ is isomorphic to $(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^s$ for some integer $s\geq 0$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4
nodes.statement:
Since  $\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb{Q}}(J_0^+(p^2))\otimes \mathbb{Q}$ is a product of totally real fields, any $u\in \operatorname{Aut}_{\mathbb{Q}}(X_0^+(p^2))$ acts as the identity or the product by $-1$ on $S_2(f)$ for $f\in\operatorname{New}_{p^2}^+$ and on $S_2(f(q)+p\varepsilon(f)f(q^p))$ for $f\in\operatorname{New}_p$.
 Hence, $\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathbb{Q}}(X_0^+(p^2))$ is isomorphic to a subgroup of $(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^r$ for $r$ equal to  $ |\operatorname{New}_{p^2}^+/G_{\mathbb{Q}}|+| \operatorname{New}_{p}/G_{\mathbb{Q}}|$. \hfill $\Box$
nodes.statement_short: Rational endomorphisms form a product of totally real fields, so a rational automorphism acts by $\pm1$ on each factor of the differentials.

nodes.name: Nontrivial automorphisms do not send infinity to a cusp
nodes.statement: If  $u$ is  a nontrivial automorphism of $X_0^+(p^2)$, then  $u(\infty)$ is not a cusp.
conclusions: $u(\infty)$ is not a cusp
nodes.label: overQ

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5
nodes.statement:
The modular curve $X_0(p^2)$ has $p+1$ cusps. Only the cusps $\infty$ and $0$ are defined over $\mathbb{Q}$. The remaining cusps $1/p,\cdots, (p-1)/p$ are defined over the $p$-th cyclotomic field $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p)$. The Galois group $\mathrm{Gal}(\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p)/\mathbb{Q})$ acts transitively on this set, and the cusp $w_{p^2}(i/p)=(p-i)/p$ is the  complex conjugate of the cusp $i/p$ (cf. \cite{Ogg}). Hence,  among the $(p+1)/2$  cusps of  $X_0^+(p^2)$  the cusp $\infty$ is the only one  defined over the quadratic field  $K$.


Let $u$ be  an  automorphism of $X_0^+(p^2)$ such that $u(\infty)$ is a cusp.   By Lemma \ref{defi},   $u(\infty)$ is defined over $K$ and, thus, $u(\infty)=\infty$.
Let $\mathbb{Q} [[q]]$ be the completion of the local ring ${\mathcal O}_{X_0^+(p^2),\infty}$ with respect to the local parameter $q$. If $u(\infty)$ is the cusp  $\infty$, then
$u^*(q)=\zeta_m q+\sum_{n>1} c_i q^i$, where $\zeta_m$ is a primitive $m$-th root of unity and, thus,  $u$ is defined over $\mathbb{Q} (\zeta_m)$. Since the unique roots of  unity in $K$ are $\pm 1$, it follows that $u$ is defined over $\mathbb{Q}$.

Now,  we will prove that, if $u\in\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathbb{Q}}(X_0^+(p^2))$ is nontrivial, then $u(\infty)\neq \infty$.  For the hyperelliptic case $p=11$, the cusp $\infty$ has $(1,4)$ as $(x,y)$ coordinates in the equation given in (\ref{eq}). Hence, $\infty$ is not a fixed point for any of the three nontrivial involutions  of $X_{0}^+(11^2)$. Let  $p>11$. Since  $X_0^+(p^2)$ is nonhyperelliptic and, by Lemma \ref{overQ}, $u$ is an involution, we can exclude the case where all eigenvalues of $u$ acting on $\Omega^1_{J_0^+(p^2)}$ are equal to $-1$ and, thus,   $u$ must have eigenvalues $1$ and $-1$ acting on this vector space.
The vector space of cusp forms $\Omega^1_{J_0^+(p^2)} {q}/{dq}$ has a basis of normalized eigenforms (see (\ref{diferencial})). Since $u$ is defined over $\mathbb{Q}$, $u$ commutes with the Hecke operators and, thus, there are two normalized eigenforms such that their corresponding regular differentials $\omega_1=(1+\sum_{n>1} a_n q^n)dq$  and $\omega_2=(1+\sum_{n>1} b_n q^n)dq$ satisfy $u^*(\omega_1)=\omega_1$ and $u^*(\omega_2)=-\omega_2$. Hence, $u$ sends $\omega_1+\omega_2$, which does vanish at $\infty$, to $\omega_1-\omega_2$, which vanishes at $\infty$.
\hfill $\Box$
nodes.statement_short: Only $\infty$ is a $K$-rational cusp, so $u(\infty)=\infty$ forces $u$ rational; then Hecke-equivariance on eigen-differentials shows a nontrivial rational involution moves $\infty$.

nodes.name: Rationality of cusps
nodes.statement: The modular curve $X_0(p^2)$ has $p+1$ cusps. Only the cusps $\infty$ and $0$ are defined over $\mathbb{Q}$. The remaining cusps $1/p,\cdots, (p-1)/p$ are defined over the $p$-th cyclotomic field $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p)$. The Galois group $\mathrm{Gal}(\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p)/\mathbb{Q})$ acts transitively on this set, and the cusp $w_{p^2}(i/p)=(p-i)/p$ is the  complex conjugate of the cusp $i/p$ (cf. \cite{Ogg}). Hence,  among the $(p+1)/2$  cusps of  $X_0^+(p^2)$  the cusp $\infty$ is the only one  defined over the quadratic field  $K$.
nodes.statement_short: Among cusps of $X_0^+(p^2)$ only $\infty$ is defined over $K$.

nodes.name: u fixes infinity
nodes.statement: Let $u$ be  an  automorphism of $X_0^+(p^2)$ such that $u(\infty)$ is a cusp.   By Lemma \ref{defi},   $u(\infty)$ is defined over $K$ and, thus, $u(\infty)=\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: By Lemma 3, $u(\infty)$ is $K$-rational, hence equals $\infty$.

nodes.name: u is rational
nodes.statement:
Let $\mathbb{Q} [[q]]$ be the completion of the local ring ${\mathcal O}_{X_0^+(p^2),\infty}$ with respect to the local parameter $q$. If $u(\infty)$ is the cusp  $\infty$, then
$u^*(q)=\zeta_m q+\sum_{n>1} c_i q^i$, where $\zeta_m$ is a primitive $m$-th root of unity and, thus,  $u$ is defined over $\mathbb{Q} (\zeta_m)$. Since the unique roots of  unity in $K$ are $\pm 1$, it follows that $u$ is defined over $\mathbb{Q}$.
nodes.statement_short: Local expansion at $\infty$ shows $u$ is defined over $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_m)\cap K=\mathbb{Q}$.

nodes.name: Remaining claim
nodes.statement: Now,  we will prove that, if $u\in\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathbb{Q}}(X_0^+(p^2))$ is nontrivial, then $u(\infty)\neq \infty$.
nodes.statement_short: It remains to show nontrivial rational automorphisms move $\infty$.

nodes.name: Case p=11
nodes.statement: For the hyperelliptic case $p=11$, the cusp $\infty$ has $(1,4)$ as $(x,y)$ coordinates in the equation given in (\ref{eq}). Hence, $\infty$ is not a fixed point for any of the three nontrivial involutions  of $X_{0}^+(11^2)$.
nodes.statement_short: On the genus-2 model $\infty=(1,4)$ is fixed by no nontrivial involution.

nodes.name: Case p>11
nodes.statement: Let  $p>11$. Since  $X_0^+(p^2)$ is nonhyperelliptic and, by Lemma \ref{overQ}, $u$ is an involution, we can exclude the case where all eigenvalues of $u$ acting on $\Omega^1_{J_0^+(p^2)}$ are equal to $-1$ and, thus,   $u$ must have eigenvalues $1$ and $-1$ acting on this vector space.
nodes.statement_short: $u$ is a non-hyperelliptic involution, so has both eigenvalues $\pm1$ on differentials.

nodes.name: Eigen-differentials argument
nodes.statement:
The vector space of cusp forms $\Omega^1_{J_0^+(p^2)} {q}/{dq}$ has a basis of normalized eigenforms (see (\ref{diferencial})). Since $u$ is defined over $\mathbb{Q}$, $u$ commutes with the Hecke operators and, thus, there are two normalized eigenforms such that their corresponding regular differentials $\omega_1=(1+\sum_{n>1} a_n q^n)dq$  and $\omega_2=(1+\sum_{n>1} b_n q^n)dq$ satisfy $u^*(\omega_1)=\omega_1$ and $u^*(\omega_2)=-\omega_2$. Hence, $u$ sends $\omega_1+\omega_2$, which does vanish at $\infty$, to $\omega_1-\omega_2$, which vanishes at $\infty$.
\hfill $\Box$
nodes.statement_short: Hecke-equivariance gives eigen-differentials $\omega_1,\omega_2$; $u$ swaps $\omega_1\pm\omega_2$, so it cannot fix $\infty$.

nodes.name: Frobenius conjugation nu
nodes.statement: Let $\nu\in\mathrm{Gal} (K/\mathbb{Q})$ be the conjugation corresponding to the Frobenius element of the prime $2$.

nodes.name: Principal divisor D_S and gonality bound
nodes.statement:
Assume that  $u\in\operatorname{Aut} (X_0^+(p^2))$ is nontrivial.  For any noncuspidal point $S\in X_0^+(p^2)({\mathbb{C}})$, the divisor
$$D_S:=(u T_2 -T_2 u^\nu)\left(\infty-S\right)\,,$$
where $T_2$ denotes de Hecke operator  viewed as a  correspondence of the curve $X_0^+(p^2)$, is nonzero but linearly
equivalent to zero.
In particular,  the $K$-gonality of $X_0^+(p^2)$ is at most $6$ and $u$ has at most $12$ fixed points.
conclusions:
is nonzero but linearly
equivalent to zero
the  $K$-gonality of $X_0^+(p^2)$ is at most $6$
$u$ has at most $12$ fixed points
nodes.statement_short: For nontrivial $u$, $D_S=(uT_2-T_2u^\nu)(\infty-S)$ is a nonzero principal divisor; hence $K$-gonality $\le6$ and $u$ has $\le12$ fixed points.
nodes.label: gonality

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6
nodes.statement:
Following the arguments used in Lemma 2.6 of \cite{KM}, one has $u\, T_2=T_2\, u^\nu$  and, thus, $D_S$ is a  principal divisor. Set $Q=u(\infty)$ and let  $P\in X_0(p^2)(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ be such that $\pi^+(P)=Q$ where $\pi^+\colon X_0(p^2)\rightarrow X_0^+(p^2)$ is the natural projection. Since $Q$ is not a cusp, there is
an elliptic curve $E$  defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ and a $p^2$-cyclic subgroup $C$ of $E(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ such that $P=(E,C)$. The other preimage of $Q$ under $\pi^+$ is the point $w_{p^2}(P)=(E/C, E[p^2]/C)$.



  If $D_S$ is a  zero divisor, then  $u T_2 (\infty)$ must be equal to $T_2 u^\nu(\infty)$ because $T_2(\infty)=3\infty$ and $\infty$ is not in the support of $T_2(S)$.  To prove that $D_S$ is a nonzero divisor,  we only need to prove that the condition $3(Q)=T_2(Q^\nu)$ cannot occur.

Let $C_i$, $1\leq i\leq 3$, be the three $2$-cyclic subgroups of $E^\nu [2]$. Since $$T_2(Q^\nu)=\sum_ {i=1}^3 \pi^+((E^\nu/C_i,  C))\,,$$ the condition $3(Q)= T_2(Q^\sigma)$  implies that each elliptic curve $E^\nu/C_i$ is isomorphic to $E$ or  $E/C$. So, at least two quotients $E^\nu/C_i$ are isomorphic and, thus, $E^\nu$ must be an elliptic curve with CM by the  order ${\mathcal O}$, where ${\mathcal O}$ is the ring of integers  $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-1}]$, $\mathbb{Z}[(1+\sqrt{-3})/2]$, $\mathbb{Z}[(1+\sqrt{-7})/2]$ or $\mathbb{Z}[(1+\sqrt{-15})/2]$. For the first three cases, $E^\nu$ is defined over $\mathbb{Q}$ and, in the last case, it is defined over $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt 5)$. In any case, $E^\nu=E$. We  prove that, in all these case, there is a subgroup $C_i$ such that $E/C_i$ has CM by the order  $2{\mathcal O}$  and this order contains an element of norm $2p^2$, which is not possible.

In the first case,  all elliptic curves $E/C_i$ are isomorphic and have CM by the order $2{\mathcal O}$. Hence, $E/C_i$ must be  isomorphic to $
E/C$  and, thus, there is a $2p^2$-cyclic isogeny from  $E/C_i$ to itself.
This leads to the existence of an element in the order $2{\mathcal O}$ of norm $2p^2$.

 In the second and third cases, $E$ is isomorphic to two curves $E/C_1$ and $E/C_2$, while $E/C_3$  is the elliptic curve with CM by $2{\mathcal O}$. Hence, $E/C_3\simeq E/C$ and, thus, we can derive the existence of an element in $2{\mathcal O}$ of norm $2p^2$.

In the last case, $E$ is defined over $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt 5)$. Two  quotients $E/C_1$ and $E/C_2$ are isomorphic to the nontrivial Galois conjugated curve of $E$, and the curve
$E/C_3$ has CM by the order $2{\mathcal O}$. Hence, $E/C_3$ is not isomorphic to $E$ and should be isomorphic to $E/C$. Again, we obtain  the existence of an element in $2{\mathcal O}$ of norm  $2 p^2$.

By taking $S=u(\infty)$, $D_S$ is defined over $K$ and, thus, the $K$-gonality is at most $6$. Finally,  since $u^*(D_S)\neq D_S$ for some noncuspidal point $S\in X_0^+(p^2)({\mathbb{C}})$,   any  nontrivial automorphism of   $X_0^+(p^2)$ has at most $12$ fixed points (cf. Lemma 3.5 of \cite{BH}).
\hfill $\Box$
nodes.statement_short: Commutation $uT_2=T_2u^\nu$ makes $D_S$ principal; if zero, $E$ would have CM by one of four orders and a quotient would give an element of norm $2p^2$ in $2\mathcal{O}$, impossible.

nodes.name: D_S principal
nodes.statement: Following the arguments used in Lemma 2.6 of \cite{KM}, one has $u\, T_2=T_2\, u^\nu$  and, thus, $D_S$ is a  principal divisor.
nodes.statement_short: As in Kenku-Momose, $uT_2=T_2u^\nu$, so $D_S$ is principal.

nodes.name: Moduli description of Q
nodes.statement:
Set $Q=u(\infty)$ and let  $P\in X_0(p^2)(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ be such that $\pi^+(P)=Q$ where $\pi^+\colon X_0(p^2)\rightarrow X_0^+(p^2)$ is the natural projection. Since $Q$ is not a cusp, there is
an elliptic curve $E$  defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ and a $p^2$-cyclic subgroup $C$ of $E(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ such that $P=(E,C)$. The other preimage of $Q$ under $\pi^+$ is the point $w_{p^2}(P)=(E/C, E[p^2]/C)$.
nodes.statement_short: Write $Q=u(\infty)$ as the image of a pair $(E,C)$ with $C$ cyclic of order $p^2$.

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement: If $D_S$ is a  zero divisor, then  $u T_2 (\infty)$ must be equal to $T_2 u^\nu(\infty)$ because $T_2(\infty)=3\infty$ and $\infty$ is not in the support of $T_2(S)$.  To prove that $D_S$ is a nonzero divisor,  we only need to prove that the condition $3(Q)=T_2(Q^\nu)$ cannot occur.
nodes.statement_short: Nonvanishing reduces to excluding $3(Q)=T_2(Q^\nu)$.

nodes.name: 2-isogenous quotients
nodes.statement:
Let $C_i$, $1\leq i\leq 3$, be the three $2$-cyclic subgroups of $E^
u [2]$. Since $$T_2(Q^
u)=\sum_ {i=1}^3 \pi^+((E^
u/C_i,  C))\,,$$ the condition $3(Q)= T_2(Q^\sigma)$  implies that each elliptic curve $E^
u/C_i$ is isomorphic to $E$ or  $E/C$.
nodes.statement_short: The condition forces each $E^\nu/C_i$ to be isomorphic to $E$ or $E/C$.

nodes.name: CM by small orders
nodes.statement: So, at least two quotients $E^\nu/C_i$ are isomorphic and, thus, $E^\nu$ must be an elliptic curve with CM by the  order ${\mathcal O}$, where ${\mathcal O}$ is the ring of integers  $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-1}]$, $\mathbb{Z}[(1+\sqrt{-3})/2]$, $\mathbb{Z}[(1+\sqrt{-7})/2]$ or $\mathbb{Z}[(1+\sqrt{-15})/2]$.
nodes.statement_short: Two isomorphic quotients force CM by one of four maximal orders.

nodes.name: E^nu = E
nodes.statement: For the first three cases, $E^\nu$ is defined over $\mathbb{Q}$ and, in the last case, it is defined over $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt 5)$. In any case, $E^\nu=E$.
nodes.statement_short: In every case $E^\nu=E$.

nodes.name: Goal for the cases
nodes.statement: We  prove that, in all these case, there is a subgroup $C_i$ such that $E/C_i$ has CM by the order  $2{\mathcal O}$  and this order contains an element of norm $2p^2$, which is not possible.
nodes.statement_short: Show some $E/C_i$ has CM by $2\mathcal{O}$ yielding an impossible element of norm $2p^2$.

nodes.name: Case Z[i]
nodes.statement:
In the first case,  all elliptic curves $E/C_i$ are isomorphic and have CM by the order $2{\mathcal O}$. Hence, $E/C_i$ must be  isomorphic to $
E/C$  and, thus, there is a $2p^2$-cyclic isogeny from  $E/C_i$ to itself.
This leads to the existence of an element in the order $2{\mathcal O}$ of norm $2p^2$.
nodes.statement_short: All quotients have CM by $2\mathcal{O}$, giving a $2p^2$-cyclic endomorphism.

nodes.name: Cases Z[zeta_3], Z[(1+sqrt-7)/2]
nodes.statement: In the second and third cases, $E$ is isomorphic to two curves $E/C_1$ and $E/C_2$, while $E/C_3$  is the elliptic curve with CM by $2{\mathcal O}$. Hence, $E/C_3\simeq E/C$ and, thus, we can derive the existence of an element in $2{\mathcal O}$ of norm $2p^2$.
nodes.statement_short: $E/C_3$ has CM by $2\mathcal{O}$ and equals $E/C$.

nodes.name: Case Z[(1+sqrt-15)/2]
nodes.statement:
In the last case, $E$ is defined over $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt 5)$. Two  quotients $E/C_1$ and $E/C_2$ are isomorphic to the nontrivial Galois conjugated curve of $E$, and the curve
$E/C_3$ has CM by the order $2{\mathcal O}$. Hence, $E/C_3$ is not isomorphic to $E$ and should be isomorphic to $E/C$. Again, we obtain  the existence of an element in $2{\mathcal O}$ of norm  $2 p^2$.
nodes.statement_short: $E/C_3$ has CM by $2\mathcal{O}$ and is isomorphic to $E/C$.

nodes.name: Gonality bound
nodes.statement: By taking $S=u(\infty)$, $D_S$ is defined over $K$ and, thus, the $K$-gonality is at most $6$.
nodes.statement_short: With $S=u(\infty)$, $D_S$ is a $K$-rational principal divisor of degree $\le6$.

nodes.name: Fixed point bound
nodes.statement:
Finally,  since $u^*(D_S)\neq D_S$ for some noncuspidal point $S\in X_0^+(p^2)({\mathbb{C}})$,   any  nontrivial automorphism of   $X_0^+(p^2)$ has at most $12$ fixed points (cf. Lemma 3.5 of \cite{BH}).
\hfill $\Box$
nodes.statement_short: By Baker-Hasegawa Lemma 3.5, $u$ has at most 12 fixed points.

nodes.name: Primes with nontrivial automorphisms
nodes.statement: If $X_0^+(p^2)$ has a nontrivial automorphism and $p>11$, then $p\in\{ 17,19,23,29,31\}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 7
nodes.statement:
By applying Lemma 3.25 of \cite{BGGP} for the prime $2$, we obtain that $$g^+ < X_0^+(p^2)(\mathbb{F}_4)+1 \,.$$ By Lemma \ref{gonality}, the $\mathbb{F}_4$-gonality of $X_0^+(p)\otimes \mathbb{F}_{4}$ is $\leq 6$ and, thus,   $X_0^+(p)(\mathbb{F}_4)\leq 30$. Hence,  $g^+\leq 30$, which implies  $p\leq 31$. The algebra $\operatorname{End}(J_0^+(13^2))\otimes\mathbb{Q} $  is a totally real number field and, thus, it only contains the roots of unity $\pm 1$. Since  $X_0^+(13^2)$ is  nonhyperelliptic,   $\operatorname{Aut}(X_0^+(13^2))$  is  trivial and  we can discard the case $p=13$.
\hfill $\Box$
nodes.statement_short: Gonality bound from Lemma 6 bounds $\mathbb{F}_4$-points, so $g^+\le30$ and $p\le31$; $p=13$ excluded since its automorphism group is trivial.

nodes.name: Point-count bound
nodes.statement: By applying Lemma 3.25 of \cite{BGGP} for the prime $2$, we obtain that $$g^+ < X_0^+(p^2)(\mathbb{F}_4)+1 \,.$$
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 3.25 of BGGP bounds $g^+$ by $\mathbb{F}_4$-points.

nodes.name: Use gonality
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{gonality}, the $\mathbb{F}_4$-gonality of $X_0^+(p)\otimes \mathbb{F}_{4}$ is $\leq 6$ and, thus,   $X_0^+(p)(\mathbb{F}_4)\leq 30$.
nodes.statement_short: Gonality $\le6$ gives at most 30 $\mathbb{F}_4$-points.

nodes.name: Bound p
nodes.statement: Hence,  $g^+\leq 30$, which implies  $p\leq 31$.
nodes.statement_short: $g^+\le30$ forces $p\le31$.

nodes.name: Exclude p=13
nodes.statement:
The algebra $\operatorname{End}(J_0^+(13^2))\otimes\mathbb{Q} $  is a totally real number field and, thus, it only contains the roots of unity $\pm 1$. Since  $X_0^+(13^2)$ is  nonhyperelliptic,   $\operatorname{Aut}(X_0^+(13^2))$  is  trivial and  we can discard the case $p=13$.
\hfill $\Box$
nodes.statement_short: For $p=13$ the automorphism group is trivial.

nodes.name: Nontrivial automorphisms have even order
nodes.statement: Every  nontrivial  automorphism  of $X_0^+(p^2)$ has  even order.
conclusions: Every  nontrivial  automorphism  of $X_0^+(p^2)$ has  even order

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 8
nodes.statement:
Assume that there is  a nontrivial  automorphism $u$ of $X_0^+(p^2)$ whose order $m$ is odd. Let $X_u$ be the quotient curve $X_0^+(p^2)/ u$  and  denote by $ g_u$ its  genus.
Next, we  find a  positive lower bound $t$ for $g_u$.
 

 The endomorphism algebra $\operatorname{End}_K(J_0^+(p^2))\otimes \mathbb{Q}$ is the product
of some noncommutative algebras and some number fields $E_f=\operatorname{End}_K (A_f)\otimes\mathbb{Q}$ attached to the  newforms $f$ lying in a certain subset ${\mathcal S}$ of $ (\operatorname{New}_{p^2}^+\cup \operatorname{New}_p)/G_{\mathbb{Q}}$. The set ${\mathcal S}$ is formed by newforms $f$ without CM such that $f\otimes \chi\notin \operatorname{New}_{p^2}^+\cup\operatorname{New}_p$ ($E_f=\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb{Q}}(A_f)$ is a totally real number field) and by a newform $f$ with CM by $K$  if $p\equiv 3\pmod 8$ ($E_f=\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb{Q}}(A_f)\otimes K$ is a CM field). For $f\in{\mathcal S}$,  the unique root of unities contained in $E_f$  are $\pm 1$. Since $m$ is odd,  the automorphism $u$ must act on each $E_f$ as the identity and, thus,  we have
$$t:= \sum_{f\in {\mathcal S}}\dim A_f\leq g_u\,.$$
 An easy  computation provides the following values for $t$:
$$
\begin{array}{c|ccccc|}
p& 17 &19 &23 & 29& 31\\\hline\hline
g^+&7 & 9& 15& 26 & 30\\
t&5 & 5& 7& 15 & 12\\ \hline

\end{array}
$$
 Applying Riemann-Hurwitz formula,
 $$\displaystyle{m\leq \frac{g^+-1}{g_u-1}\leq \frac{g^+-1}{t-1}}<3\,,$$which yields a contradiction.
\hfill $\Box$
nodes.statement_short: An odd-order automorphism acts trivially on factors with only $\pm1$ roots of unity, bounding the quotient genus below by $t$; Riemann-Hurwitz then gives $m<3$.

nodes.name: Odd-order automorphism
nodes.statement: Assume that there is  a nontrivial  automorphism $u$ of $X_0^+(p^2)$ whose order $m$ is odd. Let $X_u$ be the quotient curve $X_0^+(p^2)/ u$  and  denote by $ g_u$ its  genus.
nodes.statement_short: Suppose $u$ has odd order $m$; let $g_u$ be the genus of $X_0^+(p^2)/u$.

nodes.name: Goal
nodes.statement: Next, we  find a  positive lower bound $t$ for $g_u$.
nodes.statement_short: Seek a lower bound $t$ for $g_u$.

nodes.statement:
The endomorphism algebra $\operatorname{End}_K(J_0^+(p^2))\otimes \mathbb{Q}$ is the product
of some noncommutative algebras and some number fields $E_f=\operatorname{End}_K (A_f)\otimes\mathbb{Q}$ attached to the  newforms $f$ lying in a certain subset ${\mathcal S}$ of $ (\operatorname{New}_{p^2}^+\cup \operatorname{New}_p)/G_{\mathbb{Q}}$. The set ${\mathcal S}$ is formed by newforms $f$ without CM such that $f\otimes \chi\notin \operatorname{New}_{p^2}^+\cup\operatorname{New}_p$ ($E_f=\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb{Q}}(A_f)$ is a totally real number field) and by a newform $f$ with CM by $K$  if $p\equiv 3\pmod 8$ ($E_f=\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb{Q}}(A_f)\otimes K$ is a CM field).
nodes.statement_short: End$_K(J_0^+)$ is a product of noncommutative algebras and fields $E_f$, $f\in\mathcal{S}$.

nodes.name: Lower bound t
nodes.statement:
For $f\in{\mathcal S}$,  the unique root of unities contained in $E_f$  are $\pm 1$. Since $m$ is odd,  the automorphism $u$ must act on each $E_f$ as the identity and, thus,  we have
$$t:= \sum_{f\in {\mathcal S}}\dim A_f\leq g_u\,.$$
nodes.statement_short: Odd order forces trivial action on each $E_f$, so $t=\sum\dim A_f\le g_u$.

nodes.name: Table of t
nodes.statement:
An easy  computation provides the following values for $t$:
$$
\begin{array}{c|ccccc|}
p& 17 &19 &23 & 29& 31\\\hline\hline
g^+&7 & 9& 15& 26 & 30\\
t&5 & 5& 7& 15 & 12\\ \hline

\end{array}
$$
nodes.statement_short: Tabulate $g^+$ and $t$ for $p=17,\dots,31$.

nodes.name: Riemann-Hurwitz contradiction
nodes.statement:
Applying Riemann-Hurwitz formula,
 $$\displaystyle{m\leq \frac{g^+-1}{g_u-1}\leq \frac{g^+-1}{t-1}}<3\,,$$which yields a contradiction.
\hfill $\Box$
nodes.statement_short: Riemann-Hurwitz gives $m<3$, contradicting odd $m>1$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement:
Assume that, for $p\in\{17,19,23,29,31\}$, there is a nontrivial  automorphism $u\in\operatorname{Aut}_K(X_0^+(p^2))$. By Lemma \ref{invo}, we can suppose that $u$ is an involution. Let  $g_u$ be the genus of the quotient curve $X_0^+(p^2)/u$.
   We  know that $u$   has at most $12$ fixed points.
 By Riemann-Hurwitz formula,  we get that the number of fixed points by $u$ must be even, say $2r$, and, moreover,
$$
g_u=\frac{g^++1-r}{2}\,,\quad 0\leq r\leq 6\,.
$$
If $g^+$ is even, then $u$ can have $2$, $6$ or $10$ ramification points, while for the case $g^+$ odd, $u$ can have $0$,  $4$, $8$ or $12$  such points.

For a prime $\ell\neq p$, the curve $X=X_0^+(p^2)$ has good reduction at $\ell$. Let  $\widetilde{X}$ be the reduction of  $X$  modulo $\ell$. We write
$$
N_{\ell}(n):=1+\ell^n-\sum_{i=1}^{2 g^+}\alpha_i^n\,,
$$
where $\alpha_1,\cdots,\alpha_{2 g^+}$ are the roots of polynomial
$$
\prod_{f\in \operatorname{New}_{p^2}^+\cup\operatorname{New}_p}(x^2-a_{\ell}(f) x+\ell)
$$
and $a_{\ell}(f)$ is the $\ell$-th Fourier coefficient of $f$. By Eichler-Shimura congruence,
$N_{\ell}(n)=|\widetilde{X}(\mathbb{F}_{\ell^n})|$.

Let $\mathfrak l$ be a prime of $K$ over $\ell$ with residue degree $s$. The reduction of $X\otimes K$ modulo $\mathfrak l$ is $\widetilde X\otimes \mathbb{F}_{\ell^s}$ which has an involution, say $\widetilde u$, with at most $2r$ fixed points.  The automorphism $\widetilde u$ acts on the set $\widetilde{X}(\mathbb{F}_{\ell^{s\, n}})$ as a permutation. If  $Q\in \cup_{i=1}^n\widetilde X(\mathbb{F}_{\ell^{ s\,i}})$, then the set ${\mathcal S}_Q=\{ \widetilde{u}^i(Q)\colon 1\leq i \leq 2\}$ is contained in $ \cup_{i=1}^n\widetilde  X(\mathbb{F}_{\ell^{ s\,i}})$ and its  cardinality  is equal to $1$ or $2$ according to $Q$ is a fixed point of  $\widetilde u$ or not. Hence,    almost all integers  $R_{\ell}(n):=|\cup_{i=1}^n\widetilde  X(\mathbb{F}_{\ell^{ s\,i}})|$, $n\geq 1$,  are equivalent to the number of fixed points of $\widetilde{u}$ mod $2$
 and, moreover, the sequence $\{R_\ell (n)\}_{n\geq 1}$    can only contain at  most   $2r$ or $2r-1$ changes of parity  depending on whether $N_{\ell}(s)$ is even or odd. In other words, the sequence of integers  $\{ P_\ell(n)\}_{n\geq 1}$ defined by
$$0\leq P_\ell (n)\leq 1\,\,\text{ and }\,\,  P_{\ell}(n)=R_{\ell}(n+1)-R_{\ell}(n)\pmod 2\,,$$
can only contain at most $2r$ or $2r-1$ ones according to  $N_{\ell^s}$ being even or odd.

Note that the integer  $R_{\ell}(n+1)-R_{\ell}(n)$ can be obtained from the sequence $\{ N_\ell (s\, n)\}$
by using
$$\widetilde X (\mathbb{F}_{\ell ^{s\,d_1}})\cap \widetilde X(\mathbb{F}_{\ell ^{s\, d_2}})=\widetilde X (\mathbb{F}_{\ell ^{s\,\gcd(d_1,d_2)}})\,,\quad\text{ and if }
d_1|d_2 \text{ then }\widetilde X (\mathbb{F}_{\ell ^{s\,d_1}})\cup \widetilde X (\mathbb{F}_{\ell ^{s\,d_2}})=\widetilde X(\mathbb{F}_{\ell^{s\,d_2}})\,.
$$
More precisely, if $\{p_1,\cdots,p_r\}$ is the set of primes dividing $n+1$ and we put $d_i=(n+1)/p_i$ for $1\leq i\leq r$, then
$$
R_{\ell}(n+1)-R_{\ell}(n)= P_\ell (s(n+1))-\sum_ {j=1}^r (-1)^{r-1} \sum_{1\leq i_1<\cdots<i_j\leq r} P_\ell (s \gcd(d_{i_1},\cdots,d_{i_j}))\,.$$


For the five possibilities for $p$, we have:

\vskip 0.2 cm
{ $p=31$:}  $g^+=30$,   $2r\leq 10$ and   $\ell=2$  splits in $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-31})$. One has
$$
N_2(1)=9\,,\qquad  \sum_{n\leq 36}P_2(n)=10\,.
$$

\vskip 0.2 cm
{$p=29$:} $g^+=26$,  $2r\leq 10$ and  $\ell=2$ is inert in $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{29})$. One has
$$
N_2(2)=42\,,\qquad  \sum_{n\leq 42}P_2(n)=11\,.
$$

\vskip 0.2 cm
{ $p=23$:}  $g^+=15$,   $2r\leq 12$ and  $\ell=2$  splits in $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-23})$. One has
$$
N_2(1)=8\,,\qquad \sum_{n\leq 38}P_2(n)=13\,.
$$


\vskip 0.2 cm
{ $p=19$:} $g^+=9$,  $2r\leq 12$ and   $\ell=2$  is inert  in $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-19})$. One has
$$N_2(2)=22\,,\qquad \sum_{n\leq 46 } P_2(n)=13\,.
$$


\vskip 0.2 cm
{ $p=17$:}  $g^+=7$,  $2r\leq 12$ and  $\ell=2$  splits in $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{17})$. One has
$$
N_2(1)=6\,,\quad\quad\sum_{n\leq 46}P_2(n)=13\,.
$$
So, we can discard the five cases considered and the statement is proved.
nodes.statement_short: Assume a $K$-involution for $p\in\{17,\dots,31\}$; parity of point counts of the reduction over $\mathbb{F}_{2^{sn}}$ bounds parity changes by the number of fixed points. Computed parity sequences exceed this bound in all five cases.

nodes.name: Assume an involution
nodes.statement: Assume that, for $p\in\{17,19,23,29,31\}$, there is a nontrivial  automorphism $u\in\operatorname{Aut}_K(X_0^+(p^2))$. By Lemma \ref{invo}, we can suppose that $u$ is an involution.

nodes.statement:
Let  $g_u$ be the genus of the quotient curve $X_0^+(p^2)/u$.
   We  know that $u$   has at most $12$ fixed points.
 By Riemann-Hurwitz formula,  we get that the number of fixed points by $u$ must be even, say $2r$, and, moreover,
$$

nodes.name: Parity of ramification
nodes.statement: If $g^+$ is even, then $u$ can have $2$, $6$ or $10$ ramification points, while for the case $g^+$ odd, $u$ can have $0$,  $4$, $8$ or $12$  such points.

For a prime $\ell\neq p$, the curve $X=X_0^+(p^2)$ has good reduction at $\ell$. Let  $\widetilde{X}$ be the reduction of  $X$  modulo $\ell$. We write
$$

nodes.statement:
By Eichler-Shimura congruence,
$N_{\ell}(n)=|\widetilde{X}(\mathbb{F}_{\ell^n})|$.

nodes.statement: Let $\mathfrak l$ be a prime of $K$ over $\ell$ with residue degree $s$. The reduction of $X\otimes K$ modulo $\mathfrak l$ is $\widetilde X\otimes \mathbb{F}_{\ell^s}$ which has an involution, say $\widetilde u$, with at most $2r$ fixed points.  The automorphism $\widetilde u$ acts on the set $\widetilde{X}(\mathbb{F}_{\ell^{s\, n}})$ as a permutation.

nodes.name: Parity changes bound
nodes.statement:
If  $Q\in \cup_{i=1}^n\widetilde X(\mathbb{F}_{\ell^{ s\,i}})$, then the set ${\mathcal S}_Q=\{ \widetilde{u}^i(Q)\colon 1\leq i \leq 2\}$ is contained in $ \cup_{i=1}^n\widetilde  X(\mathbb{F}_{\ell^{ s\,i}})$ and its  cardinality  is equal to $1$ or $2$ according to $Q$ is a fixed point of  $\widetilde u$ or not. Hence,    almost all integers  $R_{\ell}(n):=|\cup_{i=1}^n\widetilde  X(\mathbb{F}_{\ell^{ s\,i}})|$, $n\geq 1$,  are equivalent to the number of fixed points of $\widetilde{u}$ mod $2$
 and, moreover, the sequence $\{R_\ell (n)\}_{n\geq 1}$    can only contain at  most   $2r$ or $2r-1$ changes of parity  depending on whether $N_{\ell}(s)$ is even or odd. In other words, the sequence of integers  $\{ P_\ell(n)\}_{n\geq 1}$ defined by
$$0\leq P_\ell (n)\leq 1\,\,\text{ and }\,\,  P_{\ell}(n)=R_{\ell}(n+1)-R_{\ell}(n)\pmod 2\,,$$
can only contain at most $2r$ or $2r-1$ ones according to  $N_{\ell^s}$ being even or odd.
nodes.statement_short: Orbit sizes 1 or 2 bound the number of parity changes of $R_\ell(n)$ by the fixed points.

nodes.name: Inclusion-exclusion for R_l
nodes.statement:
Note that the integer  $R_{\ell}(n+1)-R_{\ell}(n)$ can be obtained from the sequence $\{ N_\ell (s\, n)\}$
by using
$$\widetilde X (\mathbb{F}_{\ell ^{s\,d_1}})\cap \widetilde X(\mathbb{F}_{\ell ^{s\, d_2}})=\widetilde X (\mathbb{F}_{\ell ^{s\,\gcd(d_1,d_2)}})\,,\quad\text{ and if }
d_1|d_2 \text{ then }\widetilde X (\mathbb{F}_{\ell ^{s\,d_1}})\cup \widetilde X (\mathbb{F}_{\ell ^{s\,d_2}})=\widetilde X(\mathbb{F}_{\ell^{s\,d_2}})\,.
$$
More precisely, if $\{p_1,\cdots,p_r\}$ is the set of primes dividing $n+1$ and we put $d_i=(n+1)/p_i$ for $1\leq i\leq r$, then
$$
R_{\ell}(n+1)-R_{\ell}(n)= P_\ell (s(n+1))-\sum_ {j=1}^r (-1)^{r-1} \sum_{1\leq i_1<\cdots<i_j\leq r} P_\ell (s \gcd(d_{i_1},\cdots,d_{i_j}))\,.$$
nodes.statement_short: Express $R_\ell(n+1)-R_\ell(n)$ from the $N_\ell(sn)$ by inclusion-exclusion over divisors.

nodes.statement: For the five possibilities for $p$, we have:
